5. TECHNOLOGY ARCHITECTURE



5.1 Technology Selection Framework



Technology selections follow a structured evaluation considering:



· Phase suitability: Works on free tier? Scales to enterprise?

· Abstraction capability: Can we abstract it behind an interface?

· Ecosystem maturity: Community, documentation, talent availability

· Operational complexity: How much overhead to run and maintain?

· Cost profile: Free tier → growth → enterprise cost trajectory

· Exit strategy: How difficult to replace if needed?



5.2 Core Technology Stack



Layer Technology Phase 1 (Free Tier) Phase 2-4 (Enterprise) Rationale

Primary Language TypeScript/Node.js ✓ ✓ Single language across frontend and backend;
excellent async/event support; large ecosystem; free-tier compatible

Backend Framework NestJS ✓ ✓ Enterprise-grade Node.js framework; native DDD support;
built-in event patterns; decorator-based; OpenAPI generation

Frontend Framework React with Next.js ✓ ✓ Industry standard; static generation for marketing
pages; SSR for dashboards; vast ecosystem

API Style REST (primary) + GraphQL (selective) ✓ ✓ REST for resource operations; GraphQL for
analytics dashboards (flexible data querying)
API Gateway Custom lightweight gateway (P1) → Kong/APISIX (P3+) Custom Express-based
Kong/APISIX Free-tier compatible in P1; enterprise-grade in P3+

Database (Primary) PostgreSQL ✓ (Supabase free tier) ✓ (RDS/Cloud SQL) Relational for content,
users, config; JSON support for flexible schemas; free tier available

Database (Cache) Redis ✓ (Upstash free tier) ✓ (ElastiCache/Memorystore) Session
management; rate limiting; content cache; pub/sub

Database (Search) PostgreSQL full-text (P1) → Elasticsearch (P3+) PostgreSQL FTS Elasticsearch
Sufficient for P1; Elasticsearch for advanced search at scale

Message Broker In-memory events (P1) → Redis Pub/Sub (P2) → RabbitMQ/Kafka (P3+) NestJS
EventEmitter Redis → RabbitMQ/Kafka Abstracted behind event bus interface; evolves with
scale

Object Storage S3-compatible (Cloudflare R2 free tier) Cloudflare R2 S3/GCS Free tier generous;
S3-compatible for portability

AI Model Access Direct API calls (P1) → Abstraction Layer OpenAI/Claude APIs Multi-provider
via abstraction Start simple; add abstraction as providers multiply

Container Runtime None (P1 serverless) → Docker → Kubernetes Serverless functions Docker →
K8s (EKS/GKE) Serverless for free tier; containers for enterprise

CI/CD GitHub Actions Free tier Self-hosted runners or managed Free tier generous; scales
adequately

IaC Pulumi (TypeScript) ✓ ✓ TypeScript IaC (same language as app); multi-cloud support

Observability OpenTelemetry + Grafana (free tier) ✓ ✓ Open standard; free tier compatible;
enterprise scalable

Secrets Management Environment variables (P1) → Vault/Cloud KMS (P3+) dotenv → encrypted
env HashiCorp Vault Pragmatic for P1; enterprise-grade later



5.3 Technology Decision: TypeScript/Node.js as Primary Language



Context: Selection of primary programming language for the platform.
Options Considered:



Option Pros Cons Verdict

TypeScript/Node.js Single language full-stack; excellent async; large AI/LLM library ecosystem;
free-tier friendly; large talent pool CPU-intensive tasks less efficient; long-running processes
need care SELECTED

Python Best AI/ML ecosystem; data science libraries; rapid development Less suitable for API
servers at scale; GIL limitations; separate frontend language Not selected for primary backend

Go Excellent performance; great concurrency; single binary deployment Smaller AI library
ecosystem; separate language for frontend; steeper learning curve Reserved for performance-
critical microservices

Java/Kotlin (Spring) Enterprise maturity; excellent performance; vast ecosystem Heavy for free
tier; slower startup; separate frontend language; over-engineered for MVP Not selected

C# (.NET) Enterprise-grade; excellent performance Azure-centric ecosystem; separate frontend;
less AI library maturity Not selected



Decision: TypeScript/Node.js as the primary language, with Go reserved for performance-
critical, resource-intensive services identified during scaling.



Rationale:



1. Full-stack unification: Same language for frontend (React/Next.js) and backend reduces
context-switching, enables code sharing (types, validation), and simplifies hiring.

2. Async-native: The event-driven architecture benefits from Node.js's event loop and native
async/await patterns.

3. AI ecosystem: Rich npm ecosystem for LLM integrations (LangChain.js, OpenAI SDK, Anthropic
SDK, Vercel AI SDK).

4. Free-tier compatibility: Node.js serverless functions have minimal cold start and memory
footprint.

5. Talent availability: Largest developer ecosystem; easier hiring.
Trade-offs:



· Python would be superior for data science and model training workloads (addressed by using
Python for offline/model-training services when needed in later phases)

· Go would provide better performance for CPU-bound processing (addressed by Go extraction
for identified hot paths)

· Single language risk: mitigated by multi-language capability in the event-driven architecture

6. INFORMATION ARCHITECTURE



6.1 Data Architecture Principles



Principle Description

Data Ownership per Context Each bounded context owns its data; other contexts access via
API/events, never direct database

Polyglot Persistence Right database for the right job; not one database for everything

Event Sourcing for Critical Data Content and provenance data use event sourcing for complete
audit trail

CQRS Where Beneficial Separate read and write models for analytics and reporting

Data Minimisation Collect and store only necessary data; PII minimised by design

Immutable Audit Trail Critical data changes produce immutable events, not destructive updates

6.4 Data Flow Patterns



```

DATA FLOW PATTERNS IN THE CONTENT PIPELINE



1. COMMAND FLOW (Synchronous)

  User/System → API Gateway → Service → Database

  Used for: Configuration changes, manual content approval, user management



2. EVENT FLOW (Asynchronous)

  Service A → Event Bus → Service B → Event Bus → Service C

  Used for: Content pipeline progression, provenance recording, analytics collection



3. QUERY FLOW (Synchronous, CQRS)

  Client → API Gateway → Query Service → Read Database (optimised for queries)

  Used for: Analytics dashboards, content search, reporting



4. STREAMING FLOW (Continuous)

  External Source → Stream Processor → Event Bus → Multiple Consumers
    Used for: Trend monitoring, social media listening, real-time analytics



5. BATCH FLOW (Scheduled)

    Scheduler → Batch Job → Process Data → Store Results

    Used for: Aggregation, reporting, model training data preparation

```

7.4 Integration Resilience Patterns



Pattern Implementation Applies To

Circuit Breaker Fail fast after N failures; auto-reset after timeout All external API calls
Retry with Backoff Exponential backoff; max retries; jitter Transient failures

Bulkhead Separate connection pools per integration Resource isolation

Rate Limiter Token bucket algorithm; per-adapter limits API quota management

Health Check Periodic connectivity validation Connection monitoring

Dead Letter Queue Failed messages captured for analysis Event processing

Idempotency Idempotency keys for all external writes Publishing, payments

Graceful Degradation Service continues with reduced functionality Non-critical integrations

Phase Containerisation Approach Orchestration

P1 Container images built for consistency; deployed as serverless functions None (serverless
platform)

P2 Containerised services for steady workloads; serverless for burst Docker Compose
(dev/staging); managed container services

P3+ All services containerised Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS)

Environment Purpose Deployment Trigger Infrastructure

Staging Pre-production validation PR merge to main Matches production (free tier P1; scaled-
down P3+)

Production Live service Approved release As per deployment architecture

Sandbox Enterprise customer testing On-demand Isolated tenant in staging

9. CLOUD STRATEGY



9.1 Cloud Provider Strategy



Phase 1 (MVP): Primary deployment on a combination of best-free-tier services.



Service Category Primary (P1) Rationale
Compute (Serverless) Vercel / Cloudflare Workers Generous free tiers; global edge deployment;
integrated with frontend hosting

Database Supabase (PostgreSQL) 500MB free; managed PostgreSQL; built-in auth

Cache Upstash (Redis) Free tier sufficient for P1; managed

Object Storage Cloudflare R2 10GB free; zero egress fees (critical for content serving)

Frontend Hosting Cloudflare Pages / Vercel Free static hosting; global CDN

CI/CD GitHub Actions 2000+ free minutes/month

Monitoring Grafana Cloud Free 10K metrics; 50GB logs; 50GB traces



Phase 2-4 (Growth → Enterprise): Primary cloud provider selected based on enterprise
requirements. Architecture remains cloud-agnostic.



Provider Strengths for Agbofa Considerations

AWS Broadest service portfolio; AI/ML services (Bedrock, SageMaker); enterprise adoption;
global reach Complexity; cost management needed

GCP Strong AI/ML (Vertex AI); Kubernetes (GKE); data analytics (BigQuery); competitive pricing
Smaller enterprise market share

Azure Enterprise relationships; OpenAI partnership; hybrid cloud; Microsoft ecosystem Some
services less mature



Recommendation: AWS as primary enterprise cloud provider (broadest services, AI capabilities,
enterprise adoption), with multi-cloud architecture enabling GCP/Azure deployment for specific
enterprise customer requirements.



9.2 Multi-Cloud Architecture

10. HYBRID CLOUD STRATEGY (FUTURE)



While not in scope for Phases 1-3, the architecture accommodates future hybrid cloud
requirements:



· Containerisation ensures portability to on-premises Kubernetes

· Cloud abstraction interfaces enable on-premises implementations

· Data sovereignty architecture supports local data storage requirements

· Air-gapped deployment capability can be developed for sensitive enterprise customers



This capability will be fully designed when enterprise customer requirements demand it
(anticipated Phase 4+).

11. MICROSERVICES VS MODULAR MONOLITH ANALYSIS



11.1 Comprehensive Analysis



Factor Modular Monolith Microservices Event-Driven Modular (Selected)
Definition Single deployable with well-defined modules Independently deployable services per
domain Modules deployable together or separately; events for communication

Deployment Unit 1 N (potentially 20+) 1 → N (as needed)

Module Communication In-process method calls Network calls (REST/gRPC) Events (async) +
APIs (sync)

Data Storage Shared database (logically separated) Database per service Shared → Dedicated
(evolutionary)

Transaction Model ACID transactions Saga pattern / eventual consistency Mixed: ACID within
module; eventual across

Development Complexity Low High Low → Medium

Operational Complexity Low Very High Low → Medium

Scaling Granularity All or nothing Per-service Per-module (when extracted)

Technology Diversity Limited Full Full (where justified)

Team Autonomy Limited (shared deployment) Full Full (when extracted)

Testing Complexity Low High Low → Medium

Debugging Complexity Low High Low → Medium

Free Tier Viability Excellent Poor (resource overhead) Excellent

Enterprise Readiness Requires redesign Already distributed Already ready (with extraction)



11.2 Recommendation



Adopt the Event-Driven Modular Architecture.



Phase 1 Implementation:



· Deploy as a cohesive application (2-3 deployment units: API + Workers + Frontend)

· Strict module boundaries enforced through code organisation and interface contracts
· Internal events via in-process event bus (NestJS EventEmitter)

· Shared database with schema-per-module separation



Phase 2 Evolution:



· Extract high-load modules into separate services (Discovery, Analytics)

· Introduce external message broker (Redis Pub/Sub or Cloud Pub/Sub)

· Begin database separation for extracted services



Phase 3+ Evolution:



· Fully distributed where scale demands

· Module boundaries aligned with bounded contexts

· Independent scaling, deployment, and technology choice per service

· Event sourcing and CQRS where beneficial

13. EVENT-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURE



13.1 Event Architecture Overview



Events are the backbone of the Agbofa Nexus AI architecture. Every significant occurrence in the
system is captured as an event, enabling loose coupling, auditability, and system evolution.



13.2 Event Taxonomy
```

EVENT CATEGORIES



1. DOMAIN EVENTS

  Business-significant occurrences within a bounded context

  Examples: ContentPieceCreated, ResearchCompleted, FactCheckPassed,

       ContentPublished, RevenueEarned



2. INTEGRATION EVENTS

  Events published for consumption by other bounded contexts

  Examples: ContentReadyForVerification, ContentApprovedForPublishing,

       PerformanceDataCollected



3. SYSTEM EVENTS

  Technical occurrences for operational purposes

  Examples: ServiceHealthChanged, RateLimitApproaching,

       AgentExecutionFailed, ConfigurationUpdated



4. PROVENANCE EVENTS

  Immutable record of every content lifecycle action

  Examples: SourceAccessed, AgentInvoked, QualityScored,

       HumanDecisionMade, ContentDisclosed



5. AUDIT EVENTS

  Security and compliance-relevant actions

  Examples: UserAuthenticated, PermissionChanged,
           DataExported, ConfigurationModified

```



13.3 Event Schema Standards



All events follow a standard envelope:



```

{

    "eventId": "uuid",           // Unique event identifier

    "eventType": "namespace.action", // e.g., "content.piece.created"

    "eventVersion": "1.0",         // Schema version

    "timestamp": "ISO8601",          // Event occurrence time

    "correlationId": "uuid",       // Links events in same pipeline execution

    "causationId": "uuid",         // Event that caused this event

    "tenantId": "string",         // Multi-tenant isolation

    "source": {

      "service": "service-name",

      "instance": "instance-id"

    },

    "payload": { ... },        // Event-specific data

    "metadata": { ... }         // Additional context

}

```



13.4 Event Bus Evolution
```

PHASE 1: IN-PROCESS EVENT BUS

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│           APPLICATION PROCESS                │

│                                  │

│ ┌─────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────────┐                   │

│ │ Module A │───      │ NestJS EventEmitter       │──       Module B│

│ └─────────┘ │ (In-Memory, Synchronous)           │ └─────────┘

│         └──────────────────────────────┘               │

│                                  │

│ • Zero infrastructure overhead               │

│ • Synchronous by default (immediate handler execution) │

│ • Lost on process restart                │

│ • Suitable for single-instance, low-throughput MVP         │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘




PHASE 2: MANAGED MESSAGE SERVICE

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│                                  │

│ ┌─────────┐        ┌──────────────────┐                │
│ │ Service A│────────       │ Redis Pub/Sub │──────                     Service B│

│ └─────────┘        │ or         │      └─────────┘

│            │ Cloud Pub/Sub │               │

│ ┌─────────┐        │           │       ┌─────────┐

│ │ Service C│────────       │ (Managed,         │──────             │ Service D│

│ └─────────┘        │ Persistent) │         └─────────┘

│            └──────────────────┘                    │

│                                    │

│ • Persistent messages (survive restarts)                   │

│ • Multiple subscribers per event                       │

│ • Managed service (low operational overhead)                       │

│ • At-least-once delivery                       │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘




PHASE 3+: ENTERPRISE EVENT STREAMING

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│                                    │

│ ┌─────────┐        ┌──────────────────┐                        │

│ │ Service A│────────       │ Apache Kafka │──────                      Service B│

│ └─────────┘        │ or         │      └─────────┘

│            │ Amazon MSK        │           │

│ ┌─────────┐        │           │       ┌─────────┐

│ │ Service C│────────       │ (Streaming,       │──────             │ Service D│
│ └─────────┘        │ Event Sourcing)│       └─────────┘

│            └──────────────────┘                 │

│                                 │

│ • Event replay from any point                   │

│ • Exactly-once semantics                    │

│ • Long-term event retention                     │

│ • Event sourcing for critical domains               │

│ • Multiple consumer groups                      │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

14. SERVICE-ORIENTED DESIGN



14.1 Service Design Principles
Principle Description

Single Responsibility Each service owns one business capability

Interface-First Service contract defined before implementation

Data Ownership Service owns its data; others access via API/events

Independent Deployability Service can be deployed without coordination (in P3+)

Observability Built-In Every service emits standard telemetry

Failure Isolation Service failure doesn't cascade

Stateless Where Possible State externalised to databases and caches



14.2 Service Decomposition Model



```

14.3 Service Tier Classification



Tier Services Characteristics

Tier 1: Critical Path Discovery, Content Generation, Verification, Publishing Must be highly
available; affects content output directly

Tier 2: Business Important Analytics, Monetisation, Brand Management Impacts business
metrics but not content output

Tier 3: Supporting Notifications, Search, Reporting Enhances experience; degradation
acceptable

Tier 4: Platform Tenant Mgmt, IAM, Configuration, Audit Foundational; all services depend on
these

own ubiquitous language, domain model, and logical boundary.

15.2 Context Relationships



```

CONTEXT RELATIONSHIP PATTERNS

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



1. PARTNERSHIP (──)

  Two contexts with mutual dependency; teams collaborate

  Example: Production Context ── Verification Context



2. CUSTOMER-SUPPLIER (──      )

  Upstream context supplies; downstream conforms

  Example: Brand Context ──       Production Context (brand rules govern production)



3. CONFORMIST (──      )

  Downstream conforms to upstream model without influence

  Example: Discovery Context ──      Production Context (accepts brief structure)



4. ANTI-CORRUPTION LAYER (─►ACL►─)

  Translation layer between different models
  Example: Publishing Context ─►ACL►─ Platform APIs (translates internal model)



5. OPEN HOST SERVICE (OHS)

  Published protocol for multiple consumers

  Example: Analytics Context provides OHS for all contexts to publish metrics



6. SHARED KERNEL (minimised)

  Shared model elements; used sparingly

  Example: ContentId, TenantId, EventEnvelope shared across contexts

```



15.3 Domain Event Contracts



```

KEY DOMAIN EVENTS ACROSS CONTEXTS



DISCOVERY CONTEXT publishes:

 → TrendDetected { trendId, topic, sources, velocity, timestamp }

 → TopicScored { topicId, score, factors, timestamp }

 → ResearchCompleted { researchId, topic, facts[], sources[], confidence }

 → ContentBriefCreated { briefId, researchId, topic, angle, keywords }



PRODUCTION CONTEXT subscribes to:

 ← ContentBriefCreated

PRODUCTION CONTEXT publishes:

 → DraftGenerated { contentId, briefId, draft, metadata }
 → ContentEdited { contentId, changes, editorAgentId }



VERIFICATION CONTEXT subscribes to:

 ← ContentEdited

VERIFICATION CONTEXT publishes:

 → FactCheckCompleted { contentId, claims[], confidenceScores }

 → PlagiarismChecked { contentId, score, matches[] }

 → QualityScored { contentId, overallScore, componentScores }

 → ContentApproved { contentId } OR HumanReviewRequired { contentId, reasons }



PUBLISHING CONTEXT subscribes to:

 ← ContentApproved

 ← HumanReviewCompleted

PUBLISHING CONTEXT publishes:

 → ContentPublished { contentId, platform, url, timestamp }

 → ContentPublishFailed { contentId, platform, error }



ANALYTICS CONTEXT subscribes to:

 ← ContentPublished

 ← ContentEngagement (from platform webhooks)

ANALYTICS CONTEXT publishes:

 → PerformanceInsight { contentId, patterns, recommendations }



PROVENANCE CONTEXT subscribes to:

 ← ALL EVENTS (records immutable lineage)

```

DEPENDENCY RULES:

─────────────────

• Services depend on Integration Hub for external access (never directly)

• Services communicate via Event Bus for async operations

• Services communicate via API Gateway for sync operations (not shown for clarity)

• Services depend on Data Layer for persistence

• No circular dependencies between services

• Shared kernel (IDs, event envelopes) is the only shared dependency

21. REQUEST LIFECYCLE



21.1 API Request Lifecycle



```

API REQUEST LIFECYCLE
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



1. CLIENT REQUEST

 Client → DNS → CDN/Load Balancer → API Gateway



2. EDGE PROCESSING

 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

 │ • TLS Termination                         │

 │ • DDoS Protection (Cloudflare/AWS Shield)               │

 │ • Rate Limiting (per IP, per API key, per tenant)       │

 │ • Request Validation (schema, size, content type)           │

 │ • Bot Detection                          │

 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



3. API GATEWAY

 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

 │ • Authentication (JWT validation / API key lookup)          │

 │ • Authorisation (RBAC check against requested resource) │

 │ • Tenant Context Resolution (tenant ID from JWT/header) │

 │ • Route Matching → Target Service                   │

 │ • Request/Response Transformation if needed                 │

 │ • API Version Resolution                      │

 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



4. SERVICE PROCESSING
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

  │ • Request Context Construction (tenant, user, correlation)│

  │ • Input Validation (domain rules)               │

  │ • Business Logic Execution                  │

  │ • Domain Event Publication                   │

  │ • Response Construction                     │

  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



5. RESPONSE PATH

  Service → API Gateway → CDN/Load Balancer → Client



6. POST-RESPONSE (Asynchronous)

  Domain Events → Event Bus → Event Handlers → Other Services

  Provenance Events → Provenance Service → Audit Store

  Metrics/Traces → Observability Pipeline → Monitoring Dashboards

```



21.2 Content Pipeline Request Lifecycle



```

CONTENT PIPELINE LIFECYCLE

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



STAGE 1: TRIGGER

 • Scheduled trigger (cron-based trend check)
 • Event trigger (manual request, external webhook, trend alert)

 • Creates PipelineExecution with correlationId



STAGE 2: DISCOVERY PHASE

 • TrendDetection: Scans configured sources

 • TopicScoring: Evaluates trends against brand strategy

 • ResearchExecution: Gathers multi-source information

 • BriefGeneration: Creates structured content brief

 • Events: TrendDetected, TopicScored, ResearchCompleted, BriefCreated



STAGE 3: PRODUCTION PHASE

 • WriterAgentInvocation: Generates content from brief

 • EditorAgentInvocation: Reviews and refines content

 • Events: DraftGenerated, ContentEdited



STAGE 4: VERIFICATION PHASE

 • FactChecking: Verifies claims against sources

 • PlagiarismCheck: Checks originality

 • QualityScoring: Calculates composite quality score

 • Routing: Auto-approve, human review, or reject

 • Events: FactCheckCompleted, QualityScored, ContentApproved/ReviewRequired



STAGE 5: TRANSFORMATION PHASE

 • PlatformAdaptation: Creates platform-specific versions

 • MediaOptimisation: Optimises images/media

 • Events: ContentAdapted
STAGE 6: PUBLISHING PHASE

 • Scheduling: Determines optimal publish time

 • Publishing: Executes platform API calls

 • StatusTracking: Monitors publish status

 • Events: ContentScheduled, ContentPublished, ContentPublishFailed



STAGE 7: POST-PUBLISHING

 • AnalyticsCollection: Gathers performance data

 • Monetisation: Applies monetisation rules

 • Optimisation: Feeds performance data back to strategy

 • Events: PerformanceCollected, RevenueEarned



EVERY STAGE:

 • Provenance Recording (immutable event for each action)

 • Observability (metrics, traces, logs)

 • Error Handling (retry, dead letter, alerting)

 • State Update (pipeline status tracking)

```

23. AI PROCESSING FLOW



23.1 AI Model Invocation Flow



```

AI MODEL INVOCATION FLOW

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



1. REQUEST INITIATION

  Pipeline Stage → Agent Orchestrator → "Invoke agent_type for content_id"



2. CONTEXT ASSEMBLY

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

  │ • Load agent configuration (model, prompt, parameters) │

  │ • Load brand guidelines and voice profile            │

  │ • Load content-specific context (brief, research, etc.) │

  │ • Load relevant memory/history                   │

  │ • Assemble final prompt with context window management │

  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



3. MODEL SELECTION
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

 │ • Check agent configuration for model preference               │

 │ • Evaluate model cascade rules (task complexity → model) │

 │ • Check model availability and rate limits         │

 │ • Select primary model; configure fallback chain               │

 │ • Estimate cost and validate against budget                │

 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



4. MODEL INVOCATION

 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

 │ • Call AI Model Adapter with assembled context                 │

 │ • Set timeout (configurable per agent type)            │

 │ • Stream response where supported                      │

 │ • Collect token usage metrics                  │

 │ • Handle errors: retry → fallback → fail           │

 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



5. RESPONSE PROCESSING

 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

 │ • Parse and validate model response                │

 │ • Extract structured data from response                │

 │ • Quality check output (basic validation)          │

 │ • Record execution metrics (tokens, latency, model)                │

 │ • Return structured result to pipeline stage           │

 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
6. POST-PROCESSING (Asynchronous)

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

  │ • Record execution in Agent Execution Log          │

  │ • Update cost attribution (tenant/brand/content)       │

  │ • Emit AgentExecutionCompleted event               │

  │ • Feed execution data to model performance analytics       │

  │ • Update prompt performance metrics (if A/B testing)       │

  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

28. INTERNAL COMMUNICATION STRATEGY



28.1 Communication Patterns Matrix



Communication Type Pattern Protocol Phase 1 Phase 3+

Sync Command Request-Response REST/HTTP ✓ ✓

Sync Query Request-Response REST/HTTP (or GraphQL) ✓ ✓

Async Event Publish-Subscribe Event Bus In-process Message Broker

Async Command Message Queue Job Queue In-process Message Broker

Streaming Continuous Stream WebSocket/SSE ✗ ✓

File Transfer Object Storage S3 API ✓ ✓

Service Discovery Registry DNS / K8s Service N/A (P1 monolith) K8s DNS

Configuration Pull-based Config Service Environment vars Config Service



28.2 Service Communication Governance



```

SERVICE COMMUNICATION RULES
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



1. SYNCHRONOUS COMMUNICATION

 • ALLOWED: API Gateway → Service

 • ALLOWED: Service → External API (via Integration Hub)

 • RESTRICTED: Service → Service (requires Architecture Board approval)

 • FORBIDDEN: Circular sync dependencies



2. ASYNCHRONOUS COMMUNICATION

 • PREFERRED: All inter-service communication

 • REQUIRED: Content pipeline stage progression

 • REQUIRED: Cross-bounded-context communication

 • REQUIRED: Notifications and alerts



3. EVENT DESIGN STANDARDS

 • All events use standard envelope

 • Events are immutable facts (past tense naming)

 • Events include correlation and causation IDs

 • Events are schema-versioned

 • Event payloads are minimised (IDs, not full objects)



4. API STANDARDS

 • RESTful design for all HTTP APIs

 • OpenAPI 3.0+ specification

 • URL-based versioning (/v1/, /v2/)
    • Consistent error format across all APIs

    • Pagination via cursor-based tokens

```

30. THIRD-PARTY SERVICES STRATEGY



30.1 Service Selection & Management



```

THIRD-PARTY SERVICE GOVERNANCE

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



PRINCIPLES:

1. Abstract behind interfaces (replaceable)

2. Monitor availability and performance

3. Have documented fallback/migration plans

4. Understand and respect rate limits

5. Track costs per service



SERVICE TIERS:



TIER 1: CRITICAL (Platform cannot function without)

 • AI Model APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic) → Multi-provider + fallback

 • Primary Database → Backups + replication

 • Authentication Service → Local auth fallback



TIER 2: IMPORTANT (Degraded function without)
 • Social Platform APIs → Queued publishing; retry

 • Object Storage → Alternative provider

 • Cache Service → Direct database fallback



TIER 3: ENHANCING (Reduced capability without)

 • News APIs → Alternative sources; reduced discovery

 • Analytics Services → Delayed processing

 • Email Service → Queued delivery



SERVICE EVALUATION CRITERIA:

• API maturity and documentation quality

• SLA and uptime history

• Pricing model alignment (free tier → enterprise)

• Data residency and compliance certifications

• Vendor lock-in risk

• Community and support quality

• Integration complexity

```

Phase 1:

 • Complex: GPT-4o / Claude Sonnet (quality-critical tasks)

 • Fallback: Alternate provider if primary unavailable



Phase 2:

 • Introduce self-hosted open-source models for high-volume routine tasks

 • Model cascade: Open-source → Cost-effective API → Premium API

 • A/B testing framework for model performance comparison



Phase 3+:

 • Fine-tuned proprietary models for brand-specific voice and quality

 • Model ensemble for critical verification tasks

 • Continuous model evaluation and automated selection optimisation

33. AI ORCHESTRATION STRATEGY



33.1 Agent Orchestration Architecture



```

AI ORCHESTRATION STRATEGY

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



ORCHESTRATION PATTERNS:



1. SEQUENTIAL ORCHESTRATION

  Agent A → Agent B → Agent C

  Use: Linear content pipeline (research → write → edit → verify)

  Implementation: Workflow engine with defined agent sequence



2. CONDITIONAL ORCHESTRATION

  Agent A → [Condition] → Agent B OR Agent C

  Use: Quality-based routing (auto-publish OR human review)
 Implementation: Decision nodes in workflow definition



3. PARALLEL ORCHESTRATION

     ┌→ Agent B

 Agent A─┤

     └→ Agent C

 Use: Multi-platform content adaptation (simultaneous adaptation for all platforms)

 Implementation: Fan-out pattern with result aggregation



4. ITERATIVE ORCHESTRATION

 Agent A → Agent B → [Check] → Agent A (if not acceptable)

 Use: Content refinement loops (edit → review → edit again if needed)

 Implementation: Loop construct with max iterations and quality gate



5. ENSEMBLE ORCHESTRATION

 Agent A ─┐

 Agent B ─┼→ Aggregator → Result

 Agent C ─┘

 Use: Critical verification (multiple fact-checkers voting)

 Implementation: Fan-out with voting/consensus aggregation



ORCHESTRATION ENGINE COMPONENTS:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ Workflow Definition Store (workflow-as-code, versioned)         │

│ Workflow Engine (executes defined workflows)                │

│ State Manager (tracks execution state, enables recovery) │
│ Agent Registry (available agents, capabilities, versions) │

│ Context Builder (assembles context for each agent)            │

│ Result Evaluator (validates agent outputs, scores quality) │

│ Error Handler (retry, fallback, dead letter, alert)       │

│ Observability (execution metrics, traces, logs)           │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

34. AI MEMORY ARCHITECTURE (HIGH-LEVEL)



34.1 Memory Types and Implementation



```

AI MEMORY ARCHITECTURE

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



MEMORY TYPES:



1. WORKING MEMORY (Short-term, per execution)

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

  │ • Current pipeline context                    │

  │ • Active content brief and research data            │

  │ • Agent conversation history within pipeline            │
 │ • Implementation: In-memory during execution                     │

 │ • Lifetime: Single pipeline execution                │

 │ • Size: Managed by context window constraints                    │

 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



2. EPISODIC MEMORY (Medium-term, per content/brand)

 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

 │ • Previous content produced (style reference)                │

 │ • Recent editorial decisions and overrides               │

 │ • Brand-specific patterns and preferences                │

 │ • Implementation: Vector store + metadata (Redis/PG)                 │

 │ • Lifetime: Configurable retention (default: 90 days) │

 │ • Size: Summarised/embedded representations                      │

 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



3. SEMANTIC MEMORY (Long-term, factual knowledge)

 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

 │ • Verified facts and their sources               │

 │ • Brand guidelines and voice profiles                │

 │ • Platform best practices and algorithm knowledge                │

 │ • Editorial rules and policies               │

 │ • Implementation: PostgreSQL + Vector embeddings                     │

 │ • Lifetime: Persistent (updated with versioning)             │

 │ • Size: Comprehensive knowledge base                     │

 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
4. PROCEDURAL MEMORY (Learned behaviours)

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

  │ • Optimised prompt templates                      │

  │ • Effective agent configurations              │

  │ • Model selection patterns                    │

  │ • Performance correlations                    │

  │ • Implementation: Analytics-derived configuration        │

  │ • Lifetime: Continuously updated                  │

  │ • Size: Configuration data                │

  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



MEMORY RETRIEVAL PATTERN:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ 1. Assemble query context (current task, brand, content type) │

│ 2. Retrieve relevant semantic memory (guidelines, facts)        │

│ 3. Retrieve relevant episodic memory (similar past content)     │

│ 4. Load procedural memory (optimised configurations)            │

│ 5. Combine into working memory context                      │

│ 6. Execute agent with assembled context                 │

│ 7. Update episodic memory with new execution results            │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

36. CONFIGURATION MANAGEMENT



```

CONFIGURATION MANAGEMENT STRATEGY

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



PRINCIPLES:

1. Externalise all configuration from code

2. Environment-specific configuration (dev, staging, prod)
3. Tenant-specific configuration with inheritance from defaults

4. Version all configuration changes

5. Validate configuration before application

6. Hot-reload where possible; restart where necessary



CONFIGURATION HIERARCHY:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│                                      │

│ 1. SYSTEM DEFAULTS (built-in, code-level fallbacks)           │

│   ▼                                        │

│ 2. ENVIRONMENT CONFIG (deployment-specific: region, endpoints) │

│   ▼                                        │

│ 3. TENANT DEFAULTS (inherited by all brands in tenant)            │

│   ▼                                        │

│ 4. BRAND CONFIG (brand-specific overrides)                │

│   ▼                                        │

│ 5. USER PREFERENCES (individual user settings)            │

│                                      │

│ Each level overrides the level above it.              │

│ Configuration changes emit ConfigurationUpdated events.               │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



CONFIGURATION CATEGORIES:

• Infrastructure Config: Database URLs, message broker endpoints

• Feature Flags: Enable/disable features per tenant/brand

• AI Configuration: Model selections, prompt versions, parameters
• Business Rules: Quality thresholds, publishing rules, monetisation

• Integration Config: API keys (reference), endpoints, rate limits

• Brand Config: Voice profiles, guidelines, content strategies



CONFIGURATION STORE (Phase Evolution):

P1: Environment variables + database config tables

P2: Configuration service with API + caching

P3+: Distributed configuration (Consul/etcd) + GitOps

```

37. SECRETS MANAGEMENT (HIGH-LEVEL)



```

SECRETS MANAGEMENT STRATEGY

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



PRINCIPLES:

1. Never hardcode secrets

2. Never commit secrets to version control

3. Secrets never appear in logs or error messages

4. Least privilege access to secrets

5. Regular secret rotation

6. Audit all secret access
SECRET TYPES:

• API Keys (AI providers, social platforms, third-party services)

• Database Credentials

• Encryption Keys

• Signing Keys (JWT, webhook signatures)

• TLS Certificates

• OAuth Client Secrets



PHASE EVOLUTION:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
┐

│                                               │

│ PHASE 1: Environment Variables (with encryption)                       │

│ ─────────────────────────────────────────────                              │

│ • Secrets stored in .env files (gitignored)                    │

│ • Deployment platform encrypted env vars (Vercel/Cloudflare secrets)           │

│ • Manual rotation                                     │

│                                               │

│ PHASE 2: Managed Secrets Service                               │

│ ──────────────────────────────────                                     │

│ • Cloud provider secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager/GCP Secret Manager) │

│ • Secrets referenced by name, resolved at runtime                      │

│ • Audit logging of secret access                           │

│ • Automated rotation for supported services                        │

│                                               │
│ PHASE 3+: Enterprise Secrets Management                        │

│ ─────────────────────────────────────                              │

│ • HashiCorp Vault or equivalent                          │

│ • Dynamic secrets (short-lived, auto-generated)                │

│ • Encryption as a Service                            │

│ • Integration with enterprise PKI                        │

│ • Comprehensive audit and compliance reporting                     │

│                                               │

└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
┘



ACCESS CONTROL:

• Services authenticate to secrets manager (IAM roles, service accounts)

• Tenant-specific secrets isolated per tenant

• Just-in-time access for human operators

• Break-glass procedures documented

 │ Phase 1: 3 social platforms                         │

 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

 │ Phase 1: <5 users                               │

 │ Phase 4: 10,000+ users per enterprise tenant                    │

 │ • Stateless API services (horizontal scaling)               │

 │ • Database read replicas for query-heavy workloads                      │
  │ • CDN for static assets and public content                │

  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

• Request latency P95 > threshold

• Queue depth > threshold

39. HIGH AVAILABILITY STRATEGY



```

HIGH AVAILABILITY ARCHITECTURE

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



Phase 1 (Free Tier):

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ • Single-region deployment (managed service HA where free)              │

│ • Database: Managed service with automated backups                  │

│ • Stateless compute: Auto-restart on failure (serverless)       │

│ • Target: 99.5% availability                    │
│ • Acceptable: Brief downtime during deployments                       │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



Phase 2 (Growth):

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ • Single region, multi-AZ deployment                  │

│ • Database: Multi-AZ with automated failover                      │

│ • Compute: Multiple instances across AZs                      │

│ • Cache: Redis with replica                       │

│ • Target: 99.9% availability                      │

│ • Acceptable: <5 minutes downtime per incident                        │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



Phase 3+ (Enterprise):

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ • Multi-region active-passive or active-active                │

│ • Database: Cross-region replication                  │

│ • Global load balancing with health checks                    │

│ • Automated failover with DNS cutover                     │

│ • Target: 99.95%+ availability (enterprise SLA)               │

│ • Target: RTO < 1 hour, RPO < 5 minutes                   │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



AVAILABILITY PATTERNS:

• Health checks at every layer (load balancer, service, dependency)

• Circuit breakers prevent cascade failures
• Graceful degradation (non-critical features disable)

• Retry with exponential backoff for transient failures

• Idempotent operations for safe retry

• Blue-green deployments for zero-downtime updates

40. FAULT TOLERANCE STRATEGY



```

FAULT TOLERANCE PATTERNS

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
┐

│               FAULT TOLERANCE LAYERS                        │

│                                             │

│ LAYER 1: INFRASTRUCTURE                                     │

│ ───────────────────────                                         │

│ • Multi-AZ deployment (P2+)                                 │

│ • Auto-scaling groups replace failed instances                      │

│ • Managed services with built-in HA (database, cache, storage)          │

│ • Health checks and auto-healing                                │

│                                             │

│ LAYER 2: APPLICATION                                    │
│ ─────────────────────                                            │

│ • Circuit breakers for all external calls                        │

│ • Timeouts on all operations (no unbounded waits)                                    │

│ • Retry with exponential backoff + jitter                            │

│ • Bulkheads isolate failures (separate pools per integration)                            │

│ • Graceful degradation (shed non-critical work)                                  │

│                                              │

│ LAYER 3: DATA                                       │

│ ─────────────                                            │

│ • Database replication and automated failover                                    │

│ • Regular automated backups with tested restore                                      │

│ • Event sourcing for critical data (replay capability)                       │

│ • Write-ahead logging for data durability                                │

│                                              │

│ LAYER 4: PIPELINE                                        │

│ ─────────────────                                            │

│ • Failed pipeline stages retry or route to dead letter queue                             │

│ • Pipeline state persisted for recovery                              │

│ • Idempotency prevents duplicate content                                     │

│ • Partial pipeline execution can be resumed                                  │

│ • Content not lost on pipeline failure                               │

│                                              │

│ LAYER 5: EXTERNAL DEPENDENCIES                                           │

│ ─────────────────────────────                                                │

│ • AI model fallback chains                                   │

│ • Platform API retry with backoff                                │
│ • Stale cache acceptable when source unavailable         │

│ • Queued operations when destination unavailable             │

└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
┘



FAULT INJECTION:

• Chaos engineering in staging environments (P2+)

• Regular failure scenario testing

• Game days for incident response practice

```

42. DISASTER RECOVERY OVERVIEW



```

DISASTER RECOVERY STRATEGY

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



RECOVERY OBJECTIVES BY PHASE:



Phase 1 (MVP):

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ RTO (Recovery Time Objective): < 4 hours          │

│ RPO (Recovery Point Objective): < 1 hour          │

│                                     │

│ Strategy: Restore from automated backups to new deployment       │

│ Backups: Daily automated; retained 30 days            │

│ Recovery: Manual procedure; documented runbook               │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Phase 2 (Growth):

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ RTO: < 2 hours                              │

│ RPO: < 15 minutes                               │

│                                         │

│ Strategy: Multi-AZ with automated failover; cross-region backups │

│ Backups: Continuous (database); daily (full system)             │

│ Recovery: Semi-automated; partially scripted                │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



Phase 3+ (Enterprise):

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ RTO: < 1 hour (configurable per tenant SLA)             │

│ RPO: < 5 minutes                                │

│                                         │

│ Strategy: Active-passive multi-region; automated failover               │

│ Backups: Continuous with point-in-time recovery                 │

│ Recovery: Automated with manual approval gate                       │

│ DR Testing: Quarterly full DR test                  │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



DISASTER SCENARIOS COVERED:

• Single service failure → Auto-healing

• Availability zone failure → Multi-AZ failover

• Region failure → Cross-region failover (P3+)
• Data corruption → Point-in-time recovery

• Accidental deletion → Backup restore

• Security breach → Clean room recovery

44. CACHING STRATEGY (HIGH-LEVEL)



```

CACHING ARCHITECTURE

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



CACHE LAYERS:



1. CDN CACHE (Edge)

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

  │ • Static assets (JS, CSS, images)                   │

  │ • Public content pages                          │

  │ • API responses (public, cacheable)                      │

  │ • Implementation: Cloudflare (P1) → CloudFront/Cloud CDN (P3+) │

  │ • TTL: Assets (1 year), Content (1 hour), API (varies)       │

  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



2. APPLICATION CACHE (Redis)

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ • Session data                              │

 │ • User permissions and roles                        │

 │ • Brand configuration                           │

 │ • Rate limiting counters                        │

 │ • Frequently accessed content                           │

 │ • Computed aggregations (dashboard data)                            │

 │ • Implementation: Redis (Upstash P1 → ElastiCache P3+)                      │

 │ • TTL: Sessions (configurable), Config (5 min), Content (varies) │

 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



3. DATABASE CACHE (PostgreSQL/Application-Level)

 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

 │ • PostgreSQL query cache                            │

 │ • ORM-level entity cache                            │

 │ • Connection pool (warm connections)                            │

 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



4. AI RESPONSE CACHE

 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

 │ • Identical or near-identical AI requests                   │

 │ • Research results for recurring topics                     │

 │ • Embedding cache for semantic search                           │

 │ • Implementation: Redis with semantic similarity matching                   │

 │ • TTL: Research (1-24 hours), Embeddings (persistent)                   │

 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
CACHE INVALIDATION STRATEGY:

• Time-based expiration (TTL) for most caches

• Event-based invalidation for configuration changes

• Cache-Aside pattern: Application manages cache population

• Write-Through for critical configuration updates

• Stale-while-revalidate for acceptable staleness scenarios



CACHE EVOLUTION:

P1: Minimal caching (CDN + basic Redis)

P2: Layered caching with invalidation events

P3+: Distributed cache with cross-region replication

QUEUE & BACKGROUND PROCESSING ARCHITECTURE

──



JOB TYPES:



1. CONTENT PIPELINE JOBS

  • Trend detection (scheduled, every 15 min)
 • Research execution (on-demand, triggered by trends)

 • Content generation (on-demand, triggered by brief)

 • Verification (on-demand, triggered by draft)

 • Adaptation (on-demand, triggered by approval)

 • Publishing (scheduled, triggered by adaptation)



2. ANALYTICS JOBS

 • Performance data collection (scheduled, hourly/daily)

 • Data aggregation (scheduled, hourly)

 • Report generation (scheduled/on-demand)

 • Insight generation (scheduled, daily)



3. MAINTENANCE JOBS

 • Data cleanup and archival

 • Index rebuilding

 • Cache warming

 • Health checks

 • Backup verification



4. NOTIFICATION JOBS

 • Email notifications

 • Webhook deliveries

 • Alert dispatches



QUEUE ARCHITECTURE:
Phase 1:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ • In-process job scheduling (NestJS Schedule / Bull)                │

│ • Synchronous pipeline execution within request context                 │

│ • Simple retry on failure                      │

│ • No persistence (lost on restart)                  │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



Phase 2:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ • Redis-backed queues (Bull/BullMQ)                         │

│ • Persistent job storage                       │

│ • Delayed jobs and scheduling                       │

│ • Job progress tracking                        │

│ • Multiple worker processes                         │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



Phase 3+:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ • Dedicated message broker (RabbitMQ/Amazon MQ)                             │

│ • Dead letter queues for failed jobs                    │

│ • Priority queues for critical operations               │

│ • Job scheduling with cron expressions                      │

│ • Distributed worker pools with auto-scaling                    │

│ • Job execution audit trail                     │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
QUEUE BEST PRACTICES:

• Idempotent job handlers

• Exponential backoff for retries

• Maximum retry limits with dead letter

• Job timeout enforcement

• Queue depth monitoring and alerting

• Separate queues per job type for isolation

 │ • Metric retention: 15 days (P1) → 13 months (P3+)                  │

 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



3. TRACING

 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

 │ • Distributed tracing across all service boundaries             │

 │ • Trace context propagation (W3C Trace Context)                     │

 │ • Span attributes: service, operation, tenant, content ID           │

 │ • AI-specific spans: model, prompt (hash), tokens, latency              │

 │ • Trace sampling: 100% errors, configurable % of success                │

 │ • Trace retention: 7 days (P1) → 30 days (P3+)              │

 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



OBSERVABILITY STACK:



Phase 1:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ • OpenTelemetry SDK (instrumentation)                       │

│ • Grafana Cloud Free (metrics, logs, traces)            │

│ • Pino/Winston for structured logging               │

│ • Basic dashboards for system health                │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



Phase 3+:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ • OpenTelemetry Collector (self-hosted)                 │

│ • Prometheus (metrics) + Grafana (dashboards)                   │

│ • Loki or Elasticsearch (logs)                  │

│ • Tempo or Jaeger (traces)                      │

│ • AlertManager for alerting                     │

│ • Custom dashboards per persona                     │

│ • AI-specific observability dashboards              │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

50. LOGGING ARCHITECTURE (HIGH-LEVEL)



```

LOGGING ARCHITECTURE

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──
LOG STRUCTURE (Standard Schema):

{

    "timestamp": "ISO8601",

    "level": "INFO",

    "service": "content-generation-service",

    "traceId": "uuid",

    "spanId": "uuid",

    "tenantId": "string",

    "correlationId": "uuid",

    "contentId": "uuid (if applicable)",

    "message": "Human-readable description",

    "data": { ... context-specific data ... },

    "error": { (if applicable)

        "message": "...",

        "stack": "...",

        "code": "..."

    }

}



LOG LEVELS:

• ERROR: System errors requiring immediate attention

• WARN: Degraded operation, approaching limits, unusual patterns

• INFO: Significant business events, state changes, key operations

• DEBUG: Detailed operational information for debugging

• TRACE: Very detailed, function-level tracing (development only)
LOG CATEGORIES:

1. ACCESS LOGS: API requests, authentication events

2. APPLICATION LOGS: Business logic execution, decisions

3. AI LOGS: Model invocations, prompts (hashed), responses, tokens

4. PIPELINE LOGS: Content pipeline stage transitions

5. ERROR LOGS: Exceptions, failures, timeouts

6. AUDIT LOGS: Security-relevant actions (also in audit system)

7. PERFORMANCE LOGS: Slow queries, latency spikes



LOG TRANSPORT:

Application → Stdout/Stderr → Log Shipper (Fluentd/Vector) → Log Aggregator → Log Store



LOG RETENTION:

P1: 14 days (Grafana Cloud Free)

P2: 30 days (managed service)

P3+: Configurable per compliance requirements (30 days to 7 years)

```

52. AUDIT STRATEGY



```

AUDIT ARCHITECTURE

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



AUDIT REQUIREMENTS:

• All security-relevant actions must be audited

• All content lifecycle actions are already in Provenance system

• Audit records must be immutable

• Audit records must be queryable for compliance

• Audit records must be exportable



AUDITABLE EVENTS:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ CATEGORY          EVENTS                        │

│ ────────         ──────                         │
│ Authentication          Login, Logout, Failed Login, MFA Challenge │

│ Authorisation          Permission Change, Role Assignment            │

│ User Management             User Create/Update/Delete/Disable            │

│ Configuration          Setting Change (what, who, when, old, new) │

│ Data Access            Export, Download, Bulk Access         │

│ Content Actions           Publish, Delete, Manual Override       │

│ API Key Management Create, Rotate, Revoke                        │

│ Tenant Management            Create, Suspend, Delete, Plan Change        │

│ Security Events        Rate Limit Exceeded, Suspicious Activity │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



AUDIT RECORD STRUCTURE:

{

    "auditId": "uuid",

    "timestamp": "ISO8601",

    "actor": {

     "type": "user|service|agent",

     "id": "string",

     "name": "string",

     "tenantId": "string"

    },

    "action": "category.action",

    "resource": {

     "type": "string",

     "id": "string"

    },
    "details": { ... action-specific data ... },

    "outcome": "success|failure",

    "clientInfo": {

      "ip": "string",

      "userAgent": "string"

    },

    "correlationId": "uuid"

}



AUDIT STORAGE:

P1: PostgreSQL audit tables (within application database)

P2: Separate audit database or schema

P3+: Dedicated audit store with immutability guarantees

         • Write-once-read-many (WORM) storage

         • Hash-chaining for tamper evidence

         • SIEM integration for enterprise customers



AUDIT RETENTION:

• Minimum 1 year (standard)

• Configurable per tenant compliance requirements

• 7 years for financial/legal compliance (P3+)

54. COST OPTIMISATION STRATEGY



```

COST OPTIMISATION ARCHITECTURE

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



COST OPTIMISATION PRINCIPLES:

1. Cost awareness designed into architecture

2. Cost attribution to tenants, brands, and features

3. Continuous cost monitoring and optimisation

4. Right-sizing resources for workload

5. Leveraging free tiers and committed use discounts



COST OPTIMISATION BY LAYER:



1. COMPUTE OPTIMISATION

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

  │ • Serverless for variable workloads (pay-per-use, zero idle)         │

  │ • Spot/preemptible instances for batch processing (P2+)              │

  │ • Reserved instances for steady baselines (P2+)              │

  │ • Right-sizing: match resources to workload              │

  │ • Auto-scaling: scale down during low demand                 │

  │ • Function warming to reduce cold starts (if needed)             │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



2. STORAGE OPTIMISATION

 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

 │ • Tiered storage: hot (SSD) → warm (HDD) → cold (archive)                 │

 │ • Lifecycle policies for automatic tiering            │

 │ • Compression for stored content                      │

 │ • Deduplication of research data                  │

 │ • Data retention policies (delete expired data)           │

 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



3. DATABASE OPTIMISATION

 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

 │ • Connection pooling to reduce connection overhead                    │

 │ • Read replicas for read-heavy workloads (scale reads)            │

 │ • Query optimisation to reduce resource usage                 │

 │ • Appropriate indexing (balance read performance vs write cost) │

 │ • Data archiving for old content                  │

 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



4. AI COST OPTIMISATION

 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

 │ • Model cascading: route to cheapest capable model                │

 │ • Response caching for identical/near-identical requests          │

 │ • Prompt optimisation (shorter prompts = fewer tokens)                │

 │ • Batch processing where APIs support it                  │
  │ • Self-hosted open-source models for high-volume tasks (P2+)          │

  │ • Token usage monitoring and alerting                     │

  │ • Per-content, per-brand, per-tenant cost attribution             │

  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



5. NETWORK OPTIMISATION

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

  │ • CDN for content delivery (reduces origin traffic)           │

  │ • Compression for API responses                       │

  │ • Efficient payload formats                      │

  │ • Regional deployment to reduce data transfer costs               │

  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



COST MONITORING:

• Real-time cost dashboards

• Cost anomaly detection and alerting

• Budget setting and enforcement

• Cost allocation tags for attribution

• Monthly cost review and optimisation cycle

```

55. FREE TIER TO ENTERPRISE MIGRATION STRATEGY



```
MIGRATION STRATEGY: FREE TIER → ENTERPRISE

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



ARCHITECTURAL APPROACH:

The architecture is designed so that migration from free tier to enterprise

requires INFRASTRUCTURE CHANGES ONLY, not code changes.



MIGRATION PATH:



Phase 1: FREE TIER (Serverless + Managed Free Services)

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

 Compute:      Serverless Functions (Vercel/Cloudflare Workers)

 Database:     Supabase Free (PostgreSQL)

 Cache:      Upstash Free (Redis)

 Storage:     Cloudflare R2 Free

 Messaging: In-process EventEmitter

 Auth:       Supabase Auth / Clerk Free

 CI/CD:      GitHub Actions Free

 Monitoring: Grafana Cloud Free



 Cost: <US$200/month




Phase 2: GROWTH (Serverless + Managed Paid Services)

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 Compute:      Serverless Functions (paid tier) + Container services

 Database:     Supabase Pro / AWS RDS

 Cache:      Upstash Pro / AWS ElastiCache

 Storage:     Cloudflare R2 / AWS S3

 Messaging: Redis Pub/Sub or Cloud Pub/Sub

 Auth:       Auth0 / Clerk Pro

 CI/CD:      GitHub Actions (paid)

 Monitoring: Grafana Cloud Pro



 Cost: US$1K-5K/month




Phase 3+: ENTERPRISE (Containerised + Dedicated Infrastructure)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

 Compute:      Kubernetes (EKS/GKE) + Serverless for burst

 Database:     RDS/Cloud SQL (Multi-AZ, read replicas)

 Cache:      ElastiCache/Memorystore (cluster mode)

 Storage:     S3/GCS (with lifecycle policies)

 Messaging: Kafka/Amazon MSK or RabbitMQ/Amazon MQ

 Auth:       Enterprise IdP integration (Okta/Azure AD)

 CI/CD:      Self-hosted runners / ArgoCD

 Monitoring: Self-hosted Grafana stack + Enterprise SIEM



 Cost: US$20K-100K+/month (scales with tenants/volume)



MIGRATION ENABLERS:
1. Infrastructure abstraction interfaces (IBlobStorage, IMessageQueue, etc.)

2. Containerised applications from day one (even if deployed as serverless)

3. Configuration externalised (change endpoints, not code)

4. Database migration scripts and rollback plans

5. Feature flags for gradual capability rollout

6. Strangler Fig pattern for component-by-component migration

```

57. MULTI-TENANT ARCHITECTURE STRATEGY



```

MULTI-TENANCY ARCHITECTURE

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
──



TENANCY MODELS:



1. SHARED INFRASTRUCTURE, LOGICAL ISOLATION (Phase 1-2)

    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

    │ • Single application instance                  │

    │ • Row-level tenant isolation in database (tenant_id column)        │

    │ • Tenant context propagated through all operations             │

    │ • Query-level filtering by tenant                  │

    │ • Cache keys include tenant prefix                     │

    │ • Rate limiting per tenant                    │

    │ • Pros: Cost-effective; simple operations                  │
 │ • Cons: Noisy neighbour risk; limited compliance isolation                 │

 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



2. SCHEMA-PER-TENANT (Phase 3 Enterprise Option)

 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

 │ • Shared database instance                       │

 │ • Separate PostgreSQL schema per tenant                        │

 │ • Application resolves schema based on tenant context                      │

 │ • Pros: Better isolation; independent backup/restore                   │

 │ • Cons: Schema management overhead; connection pooling complex │

 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



3. DATABASE-PER-TENANT (Phase 3 Enterprise Premium)

 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

 │ • Separate database instance per tenant                    │

 │ • Connection pool per tenant database                  │

 │ • Pros: Maximum isolation; compliance-friendly                     │

 │ • Cons: Higher cost; operational complexity                │

 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



4. DEDICATED INFRASTRUCTURE (Phase 4 Enterprise Premium)

 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

 │ • Fully dedicated deployment per tenant                    │

 │ • Separate K8s namespace or cluster                    │

 │ • Separate data stores, cache, everything              │

 │ • Pros: Complete isolation; custom SLAs; data residency                    │
    │ • Cons: Highest cost; per-tenant operations overhead            │

    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



TENANT ISOLATION ENFORCEMENT:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│                                        │

│ LAYER           ISOLATION MECHANISM                         │

│ ─────           ──────────────────                      │

│ Application       Tenant context from JWT/API key               │

│ Service         Tenant ID in all service calls      │

│ Database          Row-level / Schema-level / Instance-level │

│ Cache           Tenant-prefixed keys                │

│ Storage          Tenant-specific prefixes/buckets           │

│ Message Queue         Tenant-specific queues or tenant header           │

│ Search          Tenant-specific indices             │

│ Observability      Tenant ID in all telemetry               │

│                                        │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘



TENANT CONTEXT PROPAGATION:

• Extracted from JWT claims or API key metadata at gateway

• Passed via standard header (X-Tenant-ID)

• Included in all event payloads

• Included in all log/metric/trace telemetry

• Enforced at data access layer (middleware/interceptor)

```

60. ARCHITECTURE DECISION RECORDS (MAJOR DECISIONS)



ADR-001: Event-Driven Modular Architecture



Field Detail

ADR ID ADR-2026-001

Date 2026-08-07

Status Accepted

Context Need to select overarching architecture style that supports free-tier MVP deployment
and enterprise scaling without redesign.

Decision Adopt Event-Driven Modular Architecture—modules with clear boundaries, event-
based communication, deployable as monolith or distributed services.

Options 1. Pure Microservices (rejected: too complex/costly for P1) 2. Modular Monolith
(rejected: limited enterprise scalability) 3. Event-Driven Modular (selected)

Rationale Enables P1 deployment as cohesive application on free tier; supports gradual
extraction to distributed services; events align naturally with AI content pipeline.

Consequences Must enforce module boundaries within shared deployment; must abstract
event bus for future externalisation; requires discipline to avoid monolith erosion.



ADR-002: TypeScript/Node.js as Primary Language



Field Detail
ADR ID ADR-2026-002

Date 2026-08-07

Status Accepted

Context Selection of primary programming language for full-stack development.

Decision TypeScript/Node.js as primary language; Go for performance-critical extracted services
when needed.

Options 1. Python (rejected: less suitable for API servers at scale) 2. Go (rejected: smaller AI
ecosystem) 3. TypeScript/Node.js (selected) 4. Java/C# (rejected: heavy for free tier)

Rationale Full-stack unification; excellent async/event support; rich AI/LLM library ecosystem;
free-tier friendly; large talent pool.

Consequences CPU-bound tasks may need Go extraction later; Python expertise needed for
potential ML training pipelines (offline).



ADR-003: PostgreSQL as Primary Database



Field Detail

ADR ID ADR-2026-003

Date 2026-08-07

Status Accepted

Context Primary data store selection for content, users, configuration, and operational data.

Decision PostgreSQL as primary database; polyglot persistence for specialised needs (Redis for
cache, S3 for assets, Elasticsearch for search at scale).

Options 1. MongoDB (rejected: less suitable for relational data; weaker ACID) 2. MySQL
(rejected: PostgreSQL has better feature set) 3. PostgreSQL (selected)

Rationale Strong ACID compliance; JSON support for flexible schemas; full-text search for P1;
free tier available (Supabase); massive ecosystem; enterprise proven.

Consequences Will need Elasticsearch at scale for advanced search; must manage connection
pooling carefully.
ADR-004: Cloud-Agnostic with Abstraction Interfaces



Field Detail

ADR ID ADR-2026-004

Date 2026-08-07

Status Accepted

Context How to balance free-tier optimisation with avoiding cloud provider lock-in.

Decision Design cloud abstraction interfaces from start; implement only what's needed for
current provider; incrementally build out multi-cloud capability.

Options 1. Full multi-cloud from day one (rejected: excessive P1 complexity) 2. Single provider
lock-in (rejected: enterprise risk) 3. Abstraction with phased implementation (selected)

Rationale Provides enterprise flexibility without over-engineering P1; interfaces define contracts
even if single implementation initially.

Consequences Additional abstraction layer complexity; must resist provider-specific feature
temptation without abstraction.



ADR-005: Event Sourcing for Content Provenance



Field Detail

ADR ID ADR-2026-005

Date 2026-08-07

Status Accepted

Context How to implement immutable content provenance and audit trail.

Decision Use event sourcing pattern for content lifecycle—all state changes captured as
immutable events; current state derived from event stream.

Options 1. Traditional CRUD with audit tables (rejected: mutable history) 2. Blockchain/DLT
(rejected: excessive complexity) 3. Event Sourcing (selected)
Rationale Immutable audit trail; complete lineage visibility; replay capability; regulatory
compliance; aligns with event-driven architecture.

Consequences Additional storage for events; eventual consistency for state projections; must
manage event schema evolution.

61. TECHNICAL RISKS



Risk ID Risk Description Likelihood Impact Mitigation

TR-1 In-process event bus insufficient for Phase 2 scale Medium Medium Abstract event bus
from day one; plan externalisation; performance test early

TR-2 Serverless cold starts impact pipeline latency Medium Medium Keep functions warm for
critical paths; accept latency for non-critical; container fallback

TR-3 PostgreSQL full-text search insufficient for Phase 2 Medium Low Plan Elasticsearch
migration; abstract search interface; P1 volumes well within PG capabilities

TR-4 Multi-tenant row-level security complexity leads to data leaks Low Critical Comprehensive
tenant isolation testing; query-level enforcement; regular security audits

TR-5 AI model API costs exceed projections at scale Medium High Model cascading; cost
monitoring; open-source model investment; cost alerting

TR-6 Eventual consistency causes data visibility issues Medium Medium Document consistency
guarantees per operation; strong consistency where needed; user education

TR-7 Module boundaries erode in shared deployment Medium High Architecture fitness
functions; dependency analysis in CI/CD; regular architecture reviews

TR-8 Cloud abstraction layer adds unacceptable complexity Low Medium Keep abstractions thin;
only abstract what needs provider flexibility; pragmatic approach
